say.text: Six years later Tikrit is still Ayyub's to keep, and the household in the citadel is waiting for a child.
Ibn Khallikan tells what came next. A woman, weeping, said that the officer of the guard had insulted her as she entered the castle gate.
Shirkuh took the officer's own halberd and struck him with it, and the man died.
It was not yours to judge, Shirkuh.
No. I did not stop to ask whose it was.
Ayyub shut his brother in a tower, and wrote to Bihruz to tell him what had happened and to put Shirkuh at his disposal.
Another account, Ibn al-Athir's, says only that Shirkuh quarrelled with a man at Tikrit and killed him. The Codex shows both.
I owe a debt to your father, who was my friend. I cannot deal harshly with either of you. But leave my service, and leave Tikrit, and seek your living where you will.
